## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning: Sampling and Generative Modelling
  Official title       Stochastic calculus in machine learning : sampling and generative modeling
  Instructors          Alain OLIVIERO-DURMUS (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 24 h (lectures 24 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Theory
  Language             Not displayed (the master-mva.com description is written in English)
  Assessment           master-mva.com (“Mode de validation”): written exam; no weighting displayed · Université Paris-Saclay: “Détail renseigné au niveau Élément Constitutif” (details given at the level of the constituent element; not displayed)
  Prerequisites        master-mva.com (“Prérequis”): “first year level knowledge in statistics and probability” · Université Paris-Saclay: not displayed
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an M2 student with a solid M1 in probability who uses Langevin samplers or diffusion models and wants to know why they work, when they fail, and how to prove it.

**Empirical first**: the unadjusted Langevin algorithm run on a standard Gaussian with step 0.5 is stable and mixes in a few dozen iterations, yet its samples have variance 1.33 instead of 1, whatever the number of iterations (ch. 7). On a two-mode target the same algorithm never leaves its starting mode, while a diffusion model driven by the exact scores recovers both modes with the right weights (ch. 8). The course explains both observations with one toolbox: Itô calculus.

The course builds stochastic calculus from Brownian motion up to stochastic differential equations, their partial differential equations and their changes of measure, then uses it to analyse two families of modern algorithms: diffusion-based Markov chain Monte Carlo and score-based generative models. It shares its objects with [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (Monte Carlo and MCMC), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) and [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (Wasserstein distances), and it prepares [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html) and [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in Artificial Intelligence](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Construct Brownian motion, prove its main invariances, and compute its quadratic variation.
-   Use continuous-time martingales: optional stopping, Doob's inequalities, convergence theorems and the quadratic variation of a local martingale.
-   Define the Itô integral through the Itô isometry, and compute stochastic integrals with Itô's formula.
-   Prove existence and uniqueness of strong solutions of Lipschitz stochastic differential equations, and simulate them with the Euler–Maruyama scheme.
-   Derive the Kolmogorov backward and Fokker–Planck equations of a diffusion, and find its invariant distribution.
-   Change the drift of a diffusion with Girsanov's theorem, write path-space likelihood ratios, and bound the Kullback–Leibler divergence between two diffusions.
-   Distinguish weak and strong solutions, and formulate a diffusion as a solution of a martingale problem.
-   Prove non-asymptotic convergence bounds for the overdamped Langevin diffusion and for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm, and explain the bias of the latter.
-   Derive the reverse-time SDE of a diffusion model, train a score by denoising score matching, and bound the error of the generated distribution.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com presents stochastic calculus as an essential tool for understanding and justifying modern machine learning techniques, such as the unadjusted Langevin algorithm and diffusion models. The course is an introduction to stochastic calculus and its applications in machine learning, with a particular focus on sampling and generative modelling.

It has two parts. The first covers the fundamentals of Itô calculus, including diffusion processes and their connections to partial differential equations. The second applies stochastic calculus to the analysis of diffusion-based MCMC methods and generative models.

The description states three objectives: present the foundational concepts of stochastic calculus and Itô calculus; develop familiarity with stochastic differential equations and diffusion processes; and apply these tools to the design and analysis of modern methods such as diffusion-based MCMC and generative models. The announced learning outcomes repeat these three points, adding the relevance of stochastic calculus in modern statistics, machine learning and applied contexts.

The description then announces eight lectures, matched item by item below. The Université Paris-Saclay course detail gives the volume (24 h of lectures, 5 ECTS) and no programme items.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites (master-mva.com): “first year level knowledge in statistics and probability”. The material assumes M1 measure-theoretic probability (conditional expectation, Gaussian vectors, modes of convergence), discrete-time martingales, and basic multivariate calculus; ch. 0 restates what is used.

-   **Preparation** — the refreshers [Probability and Statistics for MVA](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization for MVA](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (gradients, Hessians, convexity, used in ch. 7) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch for MVA](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (the code of ch. 1–8).
-   **Related courses in semester 1** — the course description names [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) and [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) as complements; [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (Wasserstein distances, used in ch. 7), [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (ULA as a noisy gradient descent), [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html) and [Mathematical Methods for Neuroscience](../s1-neuroscience-maths/index.html) (stochastic models of neurons) share tools with it.
-   **Courses that build on it in semester 2** — the description also names [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html) and [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html) (“Modèles génératifs pour l’image”). Further uses: [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in Artificial Intelligence](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html), [Inverse Problems and Imaging: Statistical and Stochastic Approaches](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) (Langevin posterior sampling), [Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis](../s2-dl-image-restoration-synthesis/index.html), [Interactions: Complexity, Stochasticity, Extrema and Rare Events](../s2-interactions/index.html), [Stopping Times and Online Algorithms](../s2-stopping-times-online/index.html) and [Learning Physical Phenomena: Metamodelling and Uncertainty Quantification](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **0. Review: conditional expectation, Gaussian vectors and discrete martingales** — the M1 tools in the form used later.
-   **1. Stochastic processes and Brownian motion** — construction, invariances, reflection principle, quadratic variation and the roughness of paths.
-   **2. Continuous-time martingales** — stopping, Doob's inequality, convergence, local martingales and the quadratic variation process.
-   **3. The Itô integral** — the isometry, its extension, integrals against continuous martingales and semimartingales.
-   **4. Itô's formula, stochastic differential equations and their PDEs** — the chain rule of stochastic calculus, strong solutions, Euler–Maruyama, Kolmogorov and Fokker–Planck equations, models from physics and biology.
-   **5. Girsanov's theorem and changes of measure** — changing the drift, likelihoods on path space, the KL divergence between two diffusions, importance sampling.
-   **6. Martingale problems, weak and strong solutions** — Tanaka's equation, the Stroock–Varadhan formulation and the Yamada–Watanabe theorems.
-   **7. Langevin dynamics and the unadjusted Langevin algorithm** — exponential convergence of the diffusion, non-asymptotic bounds for ULA, its limitations and extensions.
-   **8. Diffusion models: generative modelling by time reversal** — forward noising, the reverse-time SDE, score matching and KL guarantees.
-   **9. Research directions and open problems** — sampling complexity, Wasserstein gradient flows, theory of diffusion models (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session: the later proofs cite its numbered results without restating them.
-   After each session, redo the proofs of the boxed theorems without notes; the written-exam proposal asks for exactly these arguments.
-   Run every code block of a chapter, then change one parameter (step size, horizon, drift) and predict the effect before running again.
-   Do the exercises of the *Practice* column right after the matching session; ★★★ exercises prepare the projects.
-   Python environment: NumPy and SciPy for ch. 1–8, PyTorch for one block of ch. 8; every block fixes its seed and runs in under 30 seconds on one CPU thread.

## 0. Review: conditional expectation, Gaussian vectors and discrete martingales {#ch0}

Stochastic calculus rests on three M1 tools: conditional expectation, Gaussian vectors and discrete-time martingales. This chapter states them in the form used later; background is in the refresher [Probability and Statistics for MVA](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html). All random variables live on a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal F, \mathbb P)$.

### 0.1 Conditional expectation

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Conditional expectation]{.tag} Let $\mathcal G \subset \mathcal F$ be a sub-σ-algebra and $X \in L^1$. The conditional expectation $\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G]$ is the almost surely unique $\mathcal G$-measurable integrable variable $Y$ such that
$$
\mathbb E[X \mathbf 1_A] = \mathbb E[Y \mathbf 1_A] \qquad \text{for all } A \in \mathcal G .
$$
For $X \in L^2$ it is the orthogonal projection of $X$ onto the closed subspace $L^2(\Omega, \mathcal G, \mathbb P)$.
:::

The rules used in every proof:

-   Tower property: if $\mathcal H \subset \mathcal G$, then
    $$
    \mathbb E[\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G] \mid \mathcal H] = \mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal H].
    $$
-   Taking out what is known: if $Z$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $ZX$ is integrable, then
    $$
    \mathbb E[ZX \mid \mathcal G] = Z\, \mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G].
    $$
-   Independence: if $X$ is independent of $\mathcal G$, then $\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G] = \mathbb E[X]$.
-   Conditional Jensen: for convex $\varphi$ with $\varphi(X)$ integrable,
    $$
    \varphi(\mathbb E[X \mid \mathcal G]) \le \mathbb E[\varphi(X) \mid \mathcal G].
    $$

### 0.2 Gaussian vectors

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Gaussian vector]{.tag} A random vector $X \in \mathbb R^d$ is Gaussian if every linear combination $\langle u, X \rangle$ is a real Gaussian variable (possibly constant). Its law is determined by its mean $m$ and covariance $\Sigma$, through the characteristic function
$$
\mathbb E\, e^{i \langle u, X \rangle} = \exp\Big( i \langle u, m \rangle - \tfrac12\, u^\top \Sigma u \Big).
$$
We write $X \sim \mathcal N(m, \Sigma)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Two facts on Gaussian vectors]{.tag}

1.  The components of a Gaussian vector are independent if and only if they are uncorrelated.
2.  If $X_n \sim \mathcal N(m_n, \sigma_n^2)$ converges in $L^2$ to $X$, then $m_n \to m$, $\sigma_n^2 \to \sigma^2$, and
    $$
    X \sim \mathcal N(m, \sigma^2).
    $$

::: proof
1.  If $\Sigma$ is diagonal, the characteristic function factorises into the product of the characteristic functions of the components, which is independence.
2.  Convergence in $L^2$ implies convergence of the means and variances, and convergence in law. The characteristic functions therefore converge to $\exp(ium - u^2\sigma^2/2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A **Gaussian process** $(X_t)_{t \ge 0}$ has Gaussian finite-dimensional marginals; its law is fixed by its mean and covariance functions. Fact 2 makes the Wiener integrals of ch. 3 Gaussian.

### 0.3 Discrete-time martingales

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Discrete martingale]{.tag} A filtration is an increasing sequence of σ-algebras $(\mathcal F_n)_{n \ge 0}$. An adapted integrable sequence $(M_n)$ is a martingale if
$$
\mathbb E[M_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] = M_n \qquad \text{for all } n,
$$
a submartingale if “$\ge$” replaces “$=$”, and a supermartingale if “$\le$” does. A stopping time is a variable $\tau \in \{0, 1, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}$ with $\{\tau = n\} \in \mathcal F_n$ for all $n$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — Optional stopping, maximal inequality, convergence]{.tag} Let $(M_n)$ be a martingale.

1.  If $\tau$ is a bounded stopping time, then $\mathbb E[M_\tau] = \mathbb E[M_0]$.
2.  (Doob) For $\lambda > 0$, and for $p > 1$,
    $$
    \mathbb P\Big(\max_{k \le n} |M_k| \ge \lambda\Big) \le \frac{\mathbb E|M_n|}{\lambda}, \qquad \mathbb E\Big[\max_{k \le n} |M_k|^p\Big] \le \Big(\frac{p}{p-1}\Big)^p \mathbb E |M_n|^p .
    $$
3.  If $\sup_n \mathbb E|M_n| < \infty$, then $M_n$ converges almost surely to an integrable limit. If $\sup_n \mathbb E[M_n^2] < \infty$, the convergence also holds in $L^2$.

::: proof
1.  If $\tau \le N$, write
    $$
    M_\tau = M_0 + \sum_{k < N} \mathbf 1_{\{\tau > k\}} (M_{k+1} - M_k).
    $$
    The event $\{\tau > k\}$ is in $\mathcal F_k$, so each term has zero mean.
2.  Let $A$ be the event on the left and $\tau$ the first $k \le n$ with $|M_k| \ge \lambda$ (or $n$).

    By Jensen, $|M|$ is a submartingale. The events $A_k = A \cap \{\tau = k\}$ lie in $\mathcal F_k$, and $|M_k| \ge \lambda$ on $A_k$, so
    $$
    \lambda\, \mathbb P(A_k) \le \mathbb E[|M_k| \mathbf 1_{A_k}] \le \mathbb E[|M_n| \mathbf 1_{A_k}].
    $$
    Summing over $k \le n$ gives $\lambda\, \mathbb P(A) \le \mathbb E[|M_n| \mathbf 1_A]$. The $L^p$ bound follows by integrating this inequality in $\lambda$ and applying Hölder's inequality.
3.  The almost-sure statement is Doob's upcrossing theorem (Revuz and Yor, ch. II). In the $L^2$ case the increments are orthogonal, so
    $$
    \mathbb E[(M_n - M_m)^2] = \mathbb E[M_n^2] - \mathbb E[M_m^2]
    $$
    for $m \le n$; this is a Cauchy sequence because $\mathbb E[M_n^2]$ increases to a finite limit. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 0**

-   Conditional expectation is an $L^2$ projection, with the tower, “taking out what is known” and independence rules.
-   A Gaussian vector is fixed by its mean and covariance; $L^2$ limits of Gaussian variables are Gaussian.
-   Martingales have constant mean at bounded stopping times, satisfy Doob's maximal inequality, and converge when bounded in $L^1$ or $L^2$.
:::

## 1. Stochastic processes and Brownian motion {#ch1}

Brownian motion drives every model of the course. This chapter constructs it, lists its symmetries, and proves the property that forces a new calculus: finite quadratic variation but infinite total variation.

### 1.1 Processes, filtrations and continuity

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Process, filtration, adaptedness]{.tag} A stochastic process is a family $X = (X_t)_{t \ge 0}$ of random variables in $\mathbb R^d$. A filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is an increasing family of sub-σ-algebras of $\mathcal F$, the information available at time $t$.

-   $X$ is **adapted** if each $X_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable.
-   $X$ is **progressively measurable** if, for every $t$, the map $(s, \omega) \mapsto X_s(\omega)$ on $[0,t] \times \Omega$ is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,t]) \otimes \mathcal F_t$. An adapted process with continuous paths is progressively measurable.
-   Two processes $X$ and $Y$ are **modifications** of each other if $\mathbb P(X_t = Y_t) = 1$ for every $t$, and **indistinguishable** if $\mathbb P(X_t = Y_t \text{ for all } t) = 1$.
:::

The finite-dimensional distributions of $X$ are the laws of the vectors $(X_{t_1}, \dots, X_{t_n})$. Two theorems of Kolmogorov turn them into a process, then into a continuous one.

::: thm
[Theorem 1.2 — Kolmogorov extension]{.tag} A family of finite-dimensional laws that is consistent (marginalising a law of the family gives the law of the family on fewer times) is the family of finite-dimensional distributions of some process.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Kolmogorov continuity criterion]{.tag} Suppose that for some $\alpha, \beta, C > 0$,
$$
\mathbb E\, |X_t - X_s|^{\alpha} \le C\, |t - s|^{1 + \beta} \qquad \text{for all } s, t \in [0, T].
$$
Then $X$ has a modification with continuous paths, which is moreover γ-Hölder continuous on $[0,T]$ for every $\gamma < \beta / \alpha$.
:::

*Proof idea.* On the dyadic grid of mesh $2^{-n}$, Markov's inequality bounds the probability that some increment exceeds $2^{-n\gamma}$ by $C\, 2^{-n(\beta - \alpha\gamma)}$, which is summable. By Borel–Cantelli, the Hölder bound holds on the grid for large $n$; chaining extends it to $[0,T]$ (Revuz and Yor, Theorem I.2.1).

### 1.2 Brownian motion

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Standard Brownian motion]{.tag} A real process $B$ is a standard Brownian motion if $B_0 = 0$, its paths are continuous, and its increments over disjoint intervals are independent, with
$$
B_t - B_s \sim \mathcal N(0,\, t - s) \qquad \text{for } s \le t .
$$
Equivalently, $B$ is a continuous centred Gaussian process with covariance $\mathrm{Cov}(B_s, B_t) = s \wedge t$.

A $d$-dimensional Brownian motion has $d$ independent standard components. It is an $(\mathcal F_t)$-Brownian motion if it is adapted and each increment $B_t - B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Existence]{.tag} Standard Brownian motion exists, and its paths are γ-Hölder continuous on every compact interval for every $\gamma < 1/2$.

::: proof
The covariance $s \wedge t$ is positive semi-definite: for times $t_1, \dots, t_n$ and reals $u_i$,
$$
\sum_{i,j} u_i u_j\, (t_i \wedge t_j) = \int_0^\infty \Big( \sum_i u_i \mathbf 1_{[0, t_i]}(r) \Big)^2 dr \ \ge 0 .
$$
Theorem 1.2 therefore gives a centred Gaussian process $X$ with this covariance. Its increments are Gaussian with variance $t-s$, so $\mathbb E|X_t - X_s|^{2p} = c_p |t-s|^p$ for every integer $p$.

Theorem 1.3 with $\alpha = 2p$ and $\beta = p - 1$ gives a continuous modification, γ-Hölder for $\gamma < (p-1)/(2p)$. Letting $p \to \infty$ covers every $\gamma < 1/2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Donsker's theorem is a constructive alternative: if $(\xi_k)$ are i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance 1, the interpolated walk $n^{-1/2} \sum_{k \le nt} \xi_k$ converges in law to $B$ on $C([0,1])$.

### 1.3 Invariances, Markov property and reflection

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.6 — Invariances and the Markov property]{.tag} Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion, $c > 0$ and $s \ge 0$. Each of the following processes is again a standard Brownian motion:

-   $-B_t$ (symmetry);
-   $c^{-1/2} B_{ct}$ (scaling);
-   $B_{s+t} - B_s$, which is moreover independent of $\sigma(B_r, r \le s)$ (simple Markov property);
-   $t B_{1/t}$ for $t > 0$, extended by $0$ at $t = 0$ (time inversion).

::: proof
Each process is a centred Gaussian process. For scaling,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(c^{-1/2}B_{cs}, c^{-1/2}B_{ct}) = c^{-1}(cs \wedge ct) = s \wedge t.
$$
For time inversion,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}(sB_{1/s}, tB_{1/t}) = st\,(1/s \wedge 1/t) = s \wedge t.
$$

Continuity at $0$ of $t B_{1/t}$ follows from the law of large numbers $B_u / u \to 0$ as $u \to \infty$. The independence in the Markov property holds because the increments after $s$ are uncorrelated with, hence independent of, the values before $s$ (Proposition 0.3). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A **stopping time** is a random time $\tau \in [0, \infty]$ such that $\{\tau \le t\} \in \mathcal F_t$ for every $t$: at each time, one knows whether it has already occurred. The hitting time $\tau_a = \inf\{t : B_t = a\}$ is one.

The events known at time $\tau$ form the σ-algebra $\mathcal F_\tau$ of the events $A$ such that $A \cap \{\tau \le t\} \in \mathcal F_t$ for every $t$ (ch. 2.1 studies both notions).

The **strong Markov property** extends the third item to stopping times: if $\tau$ is an almost surely finite stopping time, then $B_{\tau + t} - B_\tau$ is a Brownian motion independent of $\mathcal F_\tau$ (Revuz and Yor, ch. III.3).

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Reflection principle]{.tag} For $a > 0$ and $t > 0$, with $S_t = \max_{s \le t} B_s$,
$$
\mathbb P(S_t \ge a) = 2\, \mathbb P(B_t \ge a) = \mathbb P(|B_t| \ge a).
$$

::: proof
Let $\tau_a$ be the first time $B$ reaches $a$, so that $\{S_t \ge a\} = \{\tau_a \le t\}$ and $B_{\tau_a} = a$.

By the strong Markov property, $B_{\tau_a + u} - a$ is a Brownian motion independent of $\mathcal F_{\tau_a}$, and by symmetry it is as likely to be above $0$ as below $0$ at time $u = t - \tau_a$. Hence
$$
\mathbb P(\tau_a \le t,\ B_t \ge a) = \tfrac12\, \mathbb P(\tau_a \le t).
$$
The left side is $\mathbb P(B_t \ge a)$, because $B_t \ge a$ forces $\tau_a \le t$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 1.4 Path regularity: the quadratic variation

Brownian paths are continuous but rough. One number measures the roughness and governs Itô calculus.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.8 — Quadratic variation of Brownian motion]{.tag} Let $\pi_n = \{0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_{k_n} = t\}$ be partitions of $[0, t]$ with mesh $|\pi_n| \to 0$. Then, in $L^2$,
$$
Q_n = \sum_i \big(B_{t_{i+1}} - B_{t_i}\big)^2 \ \longrightarrow\ t .
$$
The convergence is almost sure when $\sum_n |\pi_n| < \infty$, for instance along dyadic partitions.

::: proof
Write $\Delta_i = B_{t_{i+1}} - B_{t_i}$ and $\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i$. The variables $\Delta_i^2 - \delta_i$ are independent and centred, and $\mathrm{Var}(\Delta_i^2) = 2 \delta_i^2$ because $\mathbb E[Z^4] = 3$ for $Z \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$. Hence
$$
\mathbb E\big[(Q_n - t)^2\big] = \sum_i 2\, \delta_i^2 \ \le\ 2t\, |\pi_n| \ \longrightarrow 0 .
$$
If $\sum_n |\pi_n| < \infty$, Chebyshev's inequality gives $\sum_n \mathbb P(|Q_n - t| > \varepsilon) < \infty$ for each $\varepsilon > 0$, and Borel–Cantelli gives almost-sure convergence. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — Brownian increments are of size $\sqrt{dt}$]{.tag}
$$
\sum_i \big(B_{t_{i+1}} - B_{t_i}\big)^2 \longrightarrow t, \qquad \text{in short} \qquad (dB_t)^2 = dt .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Corollary 1.9 — Infinite variation]{.tag} Almost surely, the paths of $B$ have infinite total variation on every interval $[s, t]$ with $s < t$.

::: proof
Along dyadic partitions of $[s,t]$,
$$
\sum_i \Delta_i^2 \ \le\ \max_i |\Delta_i| \cdot \sum_i |\Delta_i| .
$$
The maximum tends to $0$ by uniform continuity of the path. If the total variation $\sum_i |\Delta_i|$ stayed bounded, the left side would tend to $0$, contradicting Theorem 1.8, which gives the limit $t - s > 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Hence $\int H_s\, dB_s$ cannot be a pathwise Stieltjes integral, and ch. 3 needs a probabilistic construction.

::: thm
[Theorem 1.10 — Hölder regularity and nowhere differentiability]{.tag} Almost surely, the paths of $B$ are γ-Hölder on compacts for every $\gamma < 1/2$ (Theorem 1.5), are not $1/2$-Hölder, and are nowhere differentiable (Paley, Wiener and Zygmund, 1933).
:::

*Proof sketch for nowhere differentiability.* If the path had a derivative bounded by $K$ at some $s \in [0,1]$, then for large $n$ three consecutive increments over intervals of length $1/n$ next to $s$ would be at most $7K/n$ in absolute value.

Each increment has density at most $\sqrt{n/2\pi}$, so a fixed position has probability at most $(14K/\sqrt{2\pi n})^3$. A union bound over the $n$ positions gives $O(n^{-1/2}) \to 0$.

::: ex
[Example 1.11 — Quadratic and total variation on one simulated path]{.tag} One path on $[0,1]$ with $2^{20}$ Gaussian increments; both variations along coarser dyadic grids.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
T, n_max = 1.0, 2 ** 20
dB = rng.standard_normal(n_max) * np.sqrt(T / n_max)    # finest increments
B = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(dB)])                # one Brownian path on [0, 1]
for k in [4, 8, 12, 16, 20]:
    incr = np.diff(B[:: n_max // 2 ** k])                 # increments on a dyadic grid of 2^k steps
    qv, tv = np.sum(incr ** 2), np.sum(np.abs(incr))
    print(f"2^{k:<2d} steps: quadratic variation {qv:.4f}   total variation {tv:7.1f}")
```

The quadratic variations, 1.0082, 0.9981, 1.0353, 1.0000 and 0.9971, stay at $t = 1$ with fluctuations of order $\sqrt{2/n}$. The total variations, 3.3, 12.8, 52.1, 204.6 and 815.2, grow like
$$
\mathbb E \sum_i |\Delta_i| = \sqrt{2n/\pi},
$$
which equals 817 for $n = 2^{20}$.
:::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 1**

-   Brownian motion is the continuous centred Gaussian process with covariance $s \wedge t$.
-   It is invariant under symmetry, scaling, time shift and time inversion, and restarts at stopping times; reflection gives the law of its maximum.
-   Its quadratic variation on $[0,t]$ is $t$: infinite variation, nowhere differentiable paths.
:::

## 2. Continuous-time martingales {#ch2}

Stochastic integrals are martingales, controlled by martingale inequalities. This chapter transfers ch. 0.3 to continuous time and introduces the quadratic variation process.

From now on, $(\mathcal F_t)$ is a filtration satisfying the usual conditions (it is right-continuous and contains the null sets), and $B$ is an $(\mathcal F_t)$-Brownian motion.

### 2.1 Martingales and stopping times

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Continuous-time martingale]{.tag} An adapted process $M$ with $\mathbb E|M_t| < \infty$ for all $t$ is a martingale if
$$
\mathbb E[M_t \mid \mathcal F_s] = M_s \qquad \text{for all } s \le t .
$$
Sub- and supermartingales are defined as in discrete time. Unless stated otherwise, the martingales of this course have continuous paths.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Three Brownian martingales]{.tag} For every $\theta \in \mathbb R$, the following processes are martingales:
$$
B_t, \qquad B_t^2 - t, \qquad \exp\big(\theta B_t - \tfrac12 \theta^2 t\big).
$$

::: proof
Write $B_t = B_s + (B_t - B_s)$, where the increment is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ with law $\mathcal N(0, t-s)$.

-   First moment: $\mathbb E[B_t \mid \mathcal F_s] = B_s + 0$.
-   Second moment: expanding the square,
    $$
    \mathbb E[B_t^2 \mid \mathcal F_s] = B_s^2 + 2B_s \cdot 0 + (t - s).
    $$
-   Exponential: by independence of the increment,
    $$
    \mathbb E[e^{\theta B_t} \mid \mathcal F_s] = e^{\theta B_s}\, \mathbb E\, e^{\theta(B_t - B_s)} = e^{\theta B_s} e^{\theta^2 (t-s)/2}.
    $$
    [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Stopping time]{.tag} A random time $\tau \in [0, \infty]$ is a stopping time if $\{\tau \le t\} \in \mathcal F_t$ for every $t$. Its σ-algebra is
$$
\mathcal F_\tau = \{ A \in \mathcal F : A \cap \{\tau \le t\} \in \mathcal F_t \text{ for all } t \}.
$$
The first time a continuous adapted process enters a closed set is a stopping time.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — Optional stopping]{.tag} Let $M$ be a continuous martingale and $\tau$ a stopping time.

1.  The stopped process $M^\tau_t = M_{t \wedge \tau}$ is a martingale.
2.  If $\tau \le T$ for a constant $T$, then
    $$
    \mathbb E[M_\tau] = \mathbb E[M_0].
    $$

::: proof
The dyadic stopping times $\tau_n = 2^{-n} \lceil 2^n \tau \rceil$ take finitely many values and decrease to $\tau$. Let $N = \lceil T \rceil + 1$, so that $\tau_n \le N$.

For $A \in \mathcal F_{\tau_n}$, the time equal to $\tau_n$ on $A$ and to $N$ off $A$ is a stopping time of the grid $2^{-n}\mathbb N$. Theorem 0.5 applied to it gives
$$
M_{\tau_n} = \mathbb E[M_N \mid \mathcal F_{\tau_n}],
$$
so the family $\{M_{\tau_n}\}$ is uniformly integrable.

Path continuity gives $M_{\tau_n} \to M_\tau$, hence part 2. Part 1 follows by applying part 2 to $\tau \wedge t$ and $\tau \wedge s$ on events of $\mathcal F_s$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Exit of Brownian motion from an interval]{.tag} Let $a, b > 0$ and let $\tau$ be the exit time of $B$ from $(-a, b)$. Then
$$
\mathbb P(B_\tau = b) = \frac{a}{a+b}, \qquad \mathbb E[\tau] = ab .
$$

::: proof
-   Optional stopping for $B_t^2 - t$ at the bounded time $\tau \wedge n$ gives
    $$
    \mathbb E[\tau \wedge n] = \mathbb E[B_{\tau \wedge n}^2] \le \max(a,b)^2.
    $$
    Monotone convergence gives $\mathbb E\tau < \infty$, so $\tau$ is finite almost surely.
-   Optional stopping for $B$ gives $\mathbb E B_{\tau \wedge n} = 0$. Since $|B_{\tau \wedge n}| \le \max(a,b)$, dominated convergence gives $\mathbb E B_\tau = 0$, that is, $b\, p - a(1-p) = 0$ with $p = \mathbb P(B_\tau = b)$.
-   Similarly $\mathbb E \tau = \mathbb E B_\tau^2 = b^2 p + a^2(1-p) = ab$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For $a = 1$, $b = 2$: $\mathbb P(B_\tau = 2) = 1/3$ and $\mathbb E\tau = 2$. An Euler simulation with step $10^{-3}$ checks this.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
a, b, dt, n_paths = 1.0, 2.0, 1e-3, 20_000
x, tau = np.zeros(n_paths), np.zeros(n_paths)
alive, t = np.ones(n_paths, dtype=bool), 0.0
while alive.any():                                        # Euler steps until every path has left (-a, b)
    t += dt
    x[alive] += np.sqrt(dt) * rng.standard_normal(alive.sum())
    out = alive & ((x <= -a) | (x >= b))
    tau[out], alive = t, alive & ~out
print(f"P(exit at b) = {np.mean(x >= b):.4f}   (exact a/(a+b) = {a / (a + b):.4f})")
print(f"E[tau]       = {tau.mean():.4f}   (exact ab = {a * b:.4f})")
```

The run prints 0.3401 and 2.0523. The exit probability is within two standard errors (0.0034) of $1/3$. The excess of $\mathbb E\tau$, four standard errors (0.013), is a discretisation bias: checking the exit only on the grid detects it late, by a time of order $\sqrt{dt}$.
::::

### 2.2 Doob's inequality and convergence

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.6 — Doob's $L^2$ inequality]{.tag} For a continuous martingale $M$ and $t \ge 0$,
$$
\mathbb E\Big[\sup_{s \le t} M_s^2\Big] \le 4\, \mathbb E\big[M_t^2\big].
$$

::: proof
Apply Theorem 0.5 (with $p = 2$) to the discrete martingale $(M_{kt2^{-n}})_{k \le 2^n}$. The maximum over the dyadic points increases with $n$ to the supremum over $[0,t]$, by continuity of the paths. Monotone convergence concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — Martingale convergence]{.tag} Let $M$ be a continuous martingale.

1.  If $\sup_t \mathbb E|M_t| < \infty$, then $M_t$ converges almost surely to an integrable variable $M_\infty$.
2.  If $\sup_t \mathbb E[M_t^2] < \infty$, the convergence also holds in $L^2$, and
    $$
    M_t = \mathbb E[M_\infty \mid \mathcal F_t] \qquad \text{for all } t.
    $$
3.  More generally, $M_t$ converges in $L^1$ if and only if $M$ is uniformly integrable, if and only if $M$ is closed by some integrable $M_\infty$ as in part 2.
:::

*Proof idea.* Doob's upcrossing inequality along dyadic times, uniform in the grid, extends to the continuous path, which therefore cannot oscillate forever. Part 2 adds Theorem 2.6 to the $L^2$ argument of Theorem 0.5 (Revuz and Yor, ch. II.2).

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — Almost-sure convergence without $L^1$ convergence]{.tag} The martingale $Z_t = \exp(B_t - t/2)$ has $\mathbb E Z_t = 1$. Yet $B_t / t \to 0$ almost surely, so the exponent $t\,(B_t/t - 1/2)$ tends to $-\infty$ and
$$
Z_t \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{almost surely}.
$$
The limit has mean 0: $(Z_t)$ is not uniformly integrable. This gap returns with Novikov's condition in ch. 5.
:::

### 2.3 Local martingales

Stochastic integrals of merely locally square-integrable integrands need not be martingales; localisation names them.

::: def
[Definition 2.9 — Continuous local martingale]{.tag} An adapted continuous process $M$ is a continuous local martingale if there are stopping times $\tau_n \uparrow \infty$ such that each stopped process $M^{\tau_n} - M_0$ is a martingale. Such $(\tau_n)$ is a localising sequence; one can always take $\tau_n = \inf\{t : |M_t - M_0| \ge n\}$.

-   A bounded continuous local martingale is a martingale (dominated convergence).
-   A nonnegative continuous local martingale with $M_0$ integrable is a supermartingale (Fatou's lemma).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.10 — Finite variation forces constancy]{.tag} A continuous local martingale whose paths have finite variation on every compact interval is constant: $M_t = M_0$ for all $t$, almost surely.

::: proof
By localisation, assume $M_0 = 0$ and that both $M$ and its total variation $V_t$ are bounded by a constant $K$. For a partition of $[0,t]$, the orthogonality of martingale increments gives
$$
\mathbb E[M_t^2] = \mathbb E \sum_i (M_{t_{i+1}} - M_{t_i})^2 \le \mathbb E\Big[ V_t \max_i |M_{t_{i+1}} - M_{t_i}| \Big].
$$
As the mesh tends to $0$, the maximum tends to $0$ by uniform continuity and stays bounded by $2K$. Dominated convergence gives $\mathbb E[M_t^2] = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 2.4 Quadratic variation and the Doob–Meyer decomposition

For Brownian motion, $B^2 - t$ is a martingale and $t$ is the quadratic variation. This holds for every continuous local martingale.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.11 — Quadratic variation of a continuous local martingale]{.tag} Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale. There is a unique continuous, increasing, adapted process $\langle M \rangle$ with $\langle M \rangle_0 = 0$ such that
$$
M_t^2 - \langle M \rangle_t \quad \text{is a continuous local martingale}.
$$
Moreover, for partitions of $[0,t]$ with mesh tending to $0$, in probability,
$$
\sum_i \big(M_{t_{i+1}} - M_{t_i}\big)^2 \longrightarrow \langle M \rangle_t .
$$

::: proof
*Uniqueness.* Let $A$ and $A'$ both qualify. Their difference $A - A'$ equals $(M^2 - A') - (M^2 - A)$, so it is a continuous local martingale. It also has finite variation and value $0$ at time $0$.

Proposition 2.10 gives $A = A'$.

*Existence.* For bounded $M$, the sums $\sum_i (M_{t_{i+1} \wedge t} - M_{t_i \wedge t})^2$ are Cauchy in $L^2$ as the mesh tends to $0$, and $M^2$ minus each sum is the martingale $M_0^2 + 2\sum_i M_{t_i}(M_{t_{i+1}} - M_{t_i})$. The limit is continuous and increasing; localisation does the rest (Revuz and Yor, Theorem IV.1.8; Le Gall, Theorem 4.9). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The **bracket** of two continuous local martingales is defined by polarisation:
$$
\langle M, N \rangle = \tfrac14 \big( \langle M + N \rangle - \langle M - N \rangle \big).
$$
It is the unique continuous finite-variation process with $\langle M, N \rangle_0 = 0$ such that $MN - \langle M, N \rangle$ is a local martingale. For a $d$-dimensional Brownian motion, $\langle B^i, B^j \rangle_t = \delta_{ij}\, t$.

::: note
[Remark 2.12 — The Doob–Meyer decomposition]{.tag} In discrete time the decomposition is explicit. An adapted integrable sequence $(X_n)$ is $X_n = X_0 + N_n + A_n$, with
$$
A_n = \sum_{k < n} \mathbb E[X_{k+1} - X_k \mid \mathcal F_k]
$$
and $N = X - X_0 - A$ a martingale null at $0$. The process $A$ is predictable ($A_{n+1}$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable), and it is increasing exactly when $X$ is a submartingale.

The decomposition is unique, because a predictable martingale null at $0$ vanishes. For $X = M^2$ with $M$ a martingale, $A_n$ is the sum of the conditional variances of the increments, the discrete analogue of $\langle M \rangle$.

Theorem 2.11 is the continuous case of the Doob–Meyer decomposition: every submartingale of class (D) is uniquely a martingale plus a predictable increasing process null at 0 (Karatzas and Shreve, Theorem 1.4.10). For $M^2$, that process is $\langle M \rangle$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.13 — $L^2$ martingales and their bracket]{.tag} Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale with $M_0 = 0$. Then $M$ is a martingale bounded in $L^2$ if and only if $\mathbb E\langle M \rangle_\infty < \infty$, and in that case
$$
\mathbb E\big[M_\infty^2\big] = \mathbb E\big[\langle M \rangle_\infty\big].
$$

::: proof
Let $\tau_n$ localise both $M$ and $M^2 - \langle M \rangle$, so that
$$
\mathbb E[M_{t \wedge \tau_n}^2] = \mathbb E\langle M \rangle_{t \wedge \tau_n}.
$$

If $\mathbb E\langle M \rangle_\infty < \infty$, Theorem 2.6 bounds $\mathbb E \sup_{s \le t} M_{s \wedge \tau_n}^2$ by $4\,\mathbb E\langle M \rangle_\infty$.

By Fatou, $\sup_s |M_s|$ is square-integrable, so $M$ is a martingale bounded in $L^2$, and the identity follows by dominated convergence. Conversely, if $M$ is a martingale bounded in $L^2$, conditional Jensen gives
$$
\mathbb E\langle M \rangle_{t \wedge \tau_n} = \mathbb E[M_{t \wedge \tau_n}^2] \le \mathbb E[M_t^2],
$$
and monotone convergence bounds $\mathbb E\langle M \rangle_\infty$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the quadratic variation compensates the square]{.tag}
$$
M_t^2 - \langle M \rangle_t \ \text{ is a local martingale}, \qquad \langle M \rangle_t = \lim \sum_i \big(M_{t_{i+1}} - M_{t_i}\big)^2 .
$$
:::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 2**

-   Optional stopping holds at bounded stopping times; with $B$ and $B^2 - t$ it solves the exit problem.
-   Doob's inequality controls the running maximum; $L^2$-bounded martingales converge and are closed by their limit, but $\exp(B_t - t/2) \to 0$ has mean 1.
-   A continuous local martingale has a quadratic variation $\langle M \rangle$ compensating $M^2$; with finite variation, it is constant.
:::

## 3. The Itô integral {#ch3}

We want to define $\int_0^t H_s\, dB_s$, the limit of $\sum_i H_{t_i} (B_{t_{i+1}} - B_{t_i})$, for random integrands $H$. Corollary 1.9 rules out a pathwise definition. Itô defines the integral as a limit in $L^2(\mathbb P)$, using one exact identity: the Itô isometry.

### 3.1 Simple integrands and the isometry

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Simple process and its integral]{.tag} A simple process is
$$
H_s = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \xi_i\, \mathbf 1_{(t_i, t_{i+1}]}(s), \qquad 0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k,
$$
where each $\xi_i$ is bounded and $\mathcal F_{t_i}$-measurable: the value used on $(t_i, t_{i+1}]$ is known at the left end point. For a continuous local martingale $M$, its integral is
$$
(H \cdot M)_t = \int_0^t H_s\, dM_s = \sum_{i} \xi_i \big( M_{t_{i+1} \wedge t} - M_{t_i \wedge t} \big).
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Itô isometry for simple integrands]{.tag} Let $H$ be simple and $M$ a continuous martingale bounded in $L^2$. Then $H \cdot M$ is a continuous martingale bounded in $L^2$, and
$$
\mathbb E\Big[ \Big( \int_0^t H_s\, dM_s \Big)^2 \Big] = \mathbb E\Big[ \int_0^t H_s^2\, d\langle M \rangle_s \Big].
$$
For $M = B$, the right side is $\mathbb E \int_0^t H_s^2\, ds$.

::: proof
Write $\Delta_i = M_{t_{i+1} \wedge t} - M_{t_i \wedge t}$.

Each term $\xi_i \Delta_i$ has conditional mean $0$ given $\mathcal F_{t_i}$, because $\xi_i$ is known at $t_i$; so $H \cdot M$ is a martingale.

-   Cross terms vanish: for $i < j$,
    $$
    \mathbb E[\xi_i \Delta_i \xi_j \Delta_j] = \mathbb E[\xi_i \Delta_i \xi_j\, \mathbb E[\Delta_j \mid \mathcal F_{t_j}]] = 0.
    $$
-   Diagonal terms: since $M^2 - \langle M \rangle$ is a martingale,
    $$
    \mathbb E[\Delta_i^2 \mid \mathcal F_{t_i}] = \mathbb E[\langle M \rangle_{t_{i+1} \wedge t} - \langle M \rangle_{t_i \wedge t} \mid \mathcal F_{t_i}].
    $$

Taking out $\xi_i^2$ and summing gives the identity. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the Itô isometry]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb E\Big[ \Big( \int_0^t H_s\, dB_s \Big)^2 \Big] = \mathbb E \int_0^t H_s^2\, ds .
$$
:::

### 3.2 Extension to square-integrable integrands

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — The spaces $L^2(M)$ and $\mathcal H^2$]{.tag} For a continuous martingale $M$ bounded in $L^2$, $L^2(M)$ is the space of progressively measurable processes with
$$
\| H \|_{L^2(M)}^2 = \mathbb E \int_0^\infty H_s^2\, d\langle M \rangle_s < \infty .
$$
$\mathcal H^2$ is the space of continuous martingales $N$ bounded in $L^2$ with $N_0 = 0$, with norm $\|N\|_{\mathcal H^2} = (\mathbb E N_\infty^2)^{1/2}$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — The Itô integral]{.tag} Simple processes are dense in $L^2(M)$. The map $H \mapsto H \cdot M$ extends uniquely to a linear isometry from $L^2(M)$ into $\mathcal H^2$. For $H \in L^2(M)$:

1.  $H \cdot M$ is a continuous martingale, with $\mathbb E[(H \cdot M)_t] = 0$;
2.  its quadratic variation is
    $$
    \langle H \cdot M \rangle_t = \int_0^t H_s^2\, d\langle M \rangle_s ;
    $$
3.  for every continuous local martingale $N$, $\langle H \cdot M, N \rangle = \int H\, d\langle M, N \rangle$, and this property characterises $H \cdot M$.

::: proof
*Density.* Let $H$ be orthogonal in $L^2(M)$ to every simple process, and let
$$
X_t = \int_0^t H_s\, d\langle M \rangle_s .
$$
Testing against $\xi \mathbf 1_{(s,t]}$ gives $\mathbb E[\xi (X_t - X_s)] = 0$ for every bounded $\mathcal F_s$-measurable $\xi$.

So $X$ is a continuous martingale of finite variation, hence $X = 0$ by Proposition 2.10, and $H = 0$ in $L^2(M)$.

*Extension.* For simple $H^n \to H$ in $L^2(M)$, the integrals $H^n \cdot M$ are Cauchy in $\mathcal H^2$ by Proposition 3.2. That space is complete: Doob's inequality (Theorem 2.6) turns $L^2$ convergence of terminal values into $L^2$ convergence of suprema, which preserves continuity. The limit does not depend on the sequence.

Properties 1 and 2 pass to the limit from simple processes; property 3 is proved in the same way (Revuz and Yor, Theorem IV.2.2). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

**Localisation.** Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale and $H$ a progressive process such that, almost surely for every $t$,
$$
\int_0^t H_s^2\, d\langle M \rangle_s < \infty .
$$
Stopping when this integral or $|M|$ exceeds $n$ reduces the construction to Theorem 3.4.

Then $H \cdot M$ is a continuous **local** martingale with the same bracket; its mean need not be $0$.

For deterministic $f \in L^2([0,t])$, the **Wiener integral** $\int_0^t f(s)\, dB_s$ is an $L^2$ limit of Gaussian variables, hence (Proposition 0.3)
$$
\int_0^t f(s)\, dB_s \sim \mathcal N\Big(0, \int_0^t f(s)^2\, ds\Big).
$$

### 3.3 Riemann sums and the role of the left end point

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — Riemann sums]{.tag} Let $H$ be continuous and adapted, and $M$ a continuous local martingale. For partitions of $[0,t]$ with mesh tending to $0$, in probability,
$$
\sum_i H_{t_i} \big(M_{t_{i+1}} - M_{t_i}\big) \longrightarrow \int_0^t H_s\, dM_s .
$$

::: proof
By localisation, assume $H$, $M$ and $\langle M \rangle$ bounded. The Riemann sum is the integral of the simple process $H^\pi = \sum_i H_{t_i} \mathbf 1_{(t_i, t_{i+1}]}$. By the isometry, its distance to $\int_0^t H\, dM$ in $L^2$ is
$$
\mathbb E \int_0^t (H^\pi_s - H_s)^2\, d\langle M \rangle_s ,
$$
which tends to $0$ by uniform continuity of $H$ on $[0,t]$ and dominated convergence. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: ex
[Example 3.6 — $\int B\, dB$ and the Stratonovich integral]{.tag} With $\Delta_i = B_{t_{i+1}} - B_{t_i}$, the algebraic identity
$$
B_{t_i} \Delta_i = \tfrac12 \big( B_{t_{i+1}}^2 - B_{t_i}^2 \big) - \tfrac12 \Delta_i^2
$$
summed over $i$, together with Proposition 3.5 and Theorem 1.8, gives
$$
\int_0^t B_s\, dB_s = \tfrac12 \big( B_t^2 - t \big).
$$

The correction $-t/2$, absent from ordinary calculus, comes from the quadratic variation; it makes the integral a martingale with mean $0$.

With the average $\frac12 (B_{t_i} + B_{t_{i+1}})$ in place of $B_{t_i}$, the sum telescopes to $\frac12 B_t^2$ exactly: the **Stratonovich integral**. It obeys the ordinary chain rule but is not a martingale; its mean is $t/2$.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, n_paths = 500, 5_000
dB = rng.standard_normal((n_paths, n)) * np.sqrt(1.0 / n)
B = np.hstack([np.zeros((n_paths, 1)), np.cumsum(dB, axis=1)])
ito = np.sum(B[:, :-1] * dB, axis=1)                      # left end points
strat = np.sum(0.5 * (B[:, :-1] + B[:, 1:]) * dB, axis=1) # average of the two end points
B1 = B[:, -1]
print(f"mean |Ito sum - (B_1^2 - 1)/2|   = {np.mean(np.abs(ito - (B1**2 - 1) / 2)):.4f}")
print(f"mean |Strat. sum - B_1^2 / 2|     = {np.mean(np.abs(strat - B1**2 / 2)):.1e}")
print(f"E[Ito integral] = {ito.mean():+.4f}   E[(Ito integral)^2] = {np.mean(ito**2):.4f}  (isometry: 0.5)")
print(f"E[Strat. integral] = {strat.mean():+.4f}")
```

With 500 steps, the Itô sums differ from $(B_1^2 - 1)/2$ by 0.025 on average (the error of the discrete quadratic variation); the averaged sums equal $B_1^2/2$ up to rounding. The Itô integral has empirical mean $-0.005$ and second moment $0.4945$, and the isometry predicts
$$
\mathbb E \int_0^1 B_s^2\, ds = \int_0^1 s\, ds = 0.5 .
$$
The Stratonovich integral has mean $0.4947$, close to $t/2 = 0.5$.
::::

### 3.4 Continuous semimartingales

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Continuous semimartingale]{.tag} A continuous semimartingale is a process
$$
X_t = X_0 + M_t + A_t ,
$$
where $M$ is a continuous local martingale and $A$ a continuous adapted process of finite variation, both null at $0$. By Proposition 2.10, the decomposition is unique.

Its quadratic variation is $\langle X \rangle = \langle M \rangle$: finite-variation parts do not contribute to sums of squares. Integrals are defined term by term,
$$
\int_0^t H_s\, dX_s = \int_0^t H_s\, dM_s + \int_0^t H_s\, dA_s ,
$$
the second integral being a pathwise Stieltjes integral.
:::

Solutions of SDEs, $X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t b_s\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma_s\, dB_s$, are continuous semimartingales with $\langle X \rangle_t = \int_0^t \sigma_s^2\, ds$.

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 3**

-   The Itô integral is the $L^2$ limit of left-point Riemann sums, built on the isometry $\mathbb E(\int H\, dB)^2 = \mathbb E \int H^2\, ds$.
-   For $H \in L^2(M)$, $H \cdot M$ is a martingale with bracket $\int H^2\, d\langle M \rangle$; otherwise a local martingale.
-   Left points give the martingale $\frac12(B_t^2 - t)$; averaged points give the Stratonovich integral $\frac12 B_t^2$.
:::

## 4. Itô's formula, stochastic differential equations and their PDEs {#ch4}

This chapter gives the chain rule of stochastic calculus and uses it to solve SDEs, to link their laws to PDEs, and to analyse two classical models of physics and biology.

### 4.1 Itô's formula

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Itô's formula]{.tag} Let $X = (X^1, \dots, X^d)$ be a vector of continuous semimartingales and $f \in C^2(\mathbb R^d)$. Then, almost surely for all $t$,
$$
f(X_t) = f(X_0) + \sum_{i} \int_0^t \partial_i f(X_s)\, dX^i_s + \frac12 \sum_{i,j} \int_0^t \partial_{ij} f(X_s)\, d\langle X^i, X^j \rangle_s .
$$
For $f \in C^{1,2}([0, \infty) \times \mathbb R^d)$, the term $\int_0^t \partial_s f(s, X_s)\, ds$ is added.

::: proof
*Sketch for $d = 1$.* By localisation, $X$, $\langle X \rangle$ and the variation of the finite-variation part are bounded, so $f''$ is uniformly continuous on the range of $X$. On a partition of $[0,t]$, Taylor's formula gives
$$
f(X_{t_{i+1}}) - f(X_{t_i}) = f'(X_{t_i})\, \Delta_i + \tfrac12 f''(\xi_i)\, \Delta_i^2 ,
$$
with $\Delta_i = X_{t_{i+1}} - X_{t_i}$ and $\xi_i$ between $X_{t_i}$ and $X_{t_{i+1}}$.

-   The first-order terms form a Riemann sum converging to $\int_0^t f'(X_s)\, dX_s$ (Proposition 3.5).
-   The sums $\sum_i f''(X_{t_i}) \Delta_i^2$ converge to $\int_0^t f''(X_s)\, d\langle X \rangle_s$, since squared increments converge to those of $\langle X \rangle$ (Theorem 2.11).
-   The remainder is at most $\max_i |f''(\xi_i) - f''(X_{t_i})| \sum_i \Delta_i^2$, a vanishing maximum times a bounded sum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In differential notation, the formula is computed with the multiplication table
$$
dt \cdot dt = 0, \qquad dt \cdot dB^i_t = 0, \qquad dB^i_t \cdot dB^j_t = \delta_{ij}\, dt .
$$
For instance $d(B_t^2) = 2 B_t\, dB_t + dt$, which is Example 3.6 again.

::: key
[Key result — Itô's formula for a diffusion]{.tag} If $dX_t = b_t\, dt + \sigma_t\, dB_t$ in $\mathbb R^d$ and $a_t = \sigma_t \sigma_t^\top$, then
$$
df(X_t) = \Big( \nabla f(X_t) \cdot b_t + \tfrac12 \operatorname{tr}\big(a_t \nabla^2 f(X_t)\big) \Big) dt + \nabla f(X_t)^\top \sigma_t\, dB_t .
$$
:::

### 4.2 Two applications

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Stochastic exponential]{.tag} Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale with $M_0 = 0$. The process
$$
\mathcal E(M)_t = \exp\big(M_t - \tfrac12 \langle M \rangle_t\big)
$$
solves $\mathcal E(M)_t = 1 + \int_0^t \mathcal E(M)_s\, dM_s$. It is a positive continuous local martingale, hence a supermartingale.

::: proof
Apply Itô's formula to $f(x, y) = e^{x - y/2}$ and the pair $(M, \langle M \rangle)$, whose second component has finite variation:
$$
d\mathcal E(M) = \mathcal E(M)\, dM - \tfrac12 \mathcal E(M)\, d\langle M \rangle + \tfrac12 \mathcal E(M)\, d\langle M \rangle = \mathcal E(M)\, dM .
$$
Definition 2.9 gives the supermartingale property. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — Lévy's characterisation of Brownian motion]{.tag} Let $M$ be a continuous local martingale in $\mathbb R^d$ with $M_0 = 0$ and $\langle M^i, M^j \rangle_t = \delta_{ij}\, t$. Then $M$ is an $(\mathcal F_t)$-Brownian motion.

::: proof
Fix $u \in \mathbb R^d$ and let
$$
Z_t = \exp\big(i \langle u, M_t \rangle + \tfrac12 |u|^2 t\big).
$$
Itô's formula, applied to real and imaginary parts, gives
$$
dZ_t = Z_t \Big( i \langle u, dM_t \rangle + \tfrac12 |u|^2 dt - \tfrac12 \sum_{j,k} u_j u_k\, d\langle M^j, M^k \rangle_t \Big) = i Z_t \langle u, dM_t \rangle .
$$
So $Z$ is a local martingale, bounded by $e^{|u|^2 T/2}$ on $[0,T]$, hence a martingale. The identity $\mathbb E[Z_t \mid \mathcal F_s] = Z_s$ reads
$$
\mathbb E\big[ e^{i \langle u, M_t - M_s \rangle} \mid \mathcal F_s \big] = e^{-|u|^2 (t-s)/2}.
$$
The increment $M_t - M_s$ is therefore independent of $\mathcal F_s$, with law $\mathcal N(0, (t-s) I_d)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Lévy's theorem recognises Brownian motions in ch. 5 and ch. 6. For moments, the Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequalities extend Doob's: for $p > 0$ and $M_0 = 0$, $\mathbb E \sup_{s \le t} |M_s|^p$ is comparable to $\mathbb E\langle M \rangle_t^{p/2}$ (Revuz and Yor, Theorem IV.4.1).

### 4.3 Stochastic differential equations: strong solutions

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Strong solution]{.tag} Let $b : \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R^d$ and $\sigma : \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R^{d \times m}$ be measurable.

Let $B$ be an $m$-dimensional $(\mathcal F_t)$-Brownian motion and $\xi$ an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable initial value.

A strong solution of
$$
dX_t = b(X_t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t)\, dB_t, \qquad X_0 = \xi,
$$
is a continuous adapted process with
$$
X_t = \xi + \int_0^t b(X_s)\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma(X_s)\, dB_s
$$
for all $t$, almost surely. **Pathwise uniqueness** holds if two solutions on the same space, with the same $B$ and $\xi$, are indistinguishable.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Existence and uniqueness under Lipschitz coefficients (Itô)]{.tag} Assume that for some $L$ and all $x, y$,
$$
|b(x) - b(y)| + \|\sigma(x) - \sigma(y)\|_F \le L\, |x - y| ,
$$
and that $\mathbb E|\xi|^2 < \infty$. Then the SDE has a pathwise unique strong solution, and $\mathbb E \sup_{t \le T} |X_t|^2 < \infty$ for every $T$.

::: proof
Fix $T$. For continuous adapted $Y$ with $\mathbb E \sup_{t \le T}|Y_t|^2 < \infty$, let
$$
\Phi(Y)_t = \xi + \int_0^t b(Y_s)\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma(Y_s)\, dB_s,
$$
which has the same integrability (linear growth).

*Key estimate.* For two such $Y, Y'$, using $(x+y)^2 \le 2x^2 + 2y^2$, Cauchy–Schwarz on the $ds$ integral, and Doob's inequality with the isometry on the $dB$ integral:
$$
\mathbb E \sup_{s \le t} |\Phi(Y)_s - \Phi(Y')_s|^2 \le K \int_0^t \mathbb E \sup_{u \le s} |Y_u - Y'_u|^2\, ds, \qquad K = 2L^2 (T + 4).
$$

*Uniqueness.* For two solutions $X, X'$ (localised), $\phi(t) = \mathbb E \sup_{s \le t} |X_s - X'_s|^2$ satisfies $\phi(t) \le K \int_0^t \phi(s)\, ds$, so $\phi = 0$ by Gronwall's lemma.

*Existence.* Let $X^0 = \xi$ and $X^{n+1} = \Phi(X^n)$. Iterating the key estimate gives
$$
\mathbb E \sup_{s \le T} |X^{n+1}_s - X^n_s|^2 \le C\, \frac{(KT)^n}{n!} .
$$
By Markov's inequality and Borel–Cantelli, $X^n$ converges uniformly on $[0,T]$, almost surely and in $L^2$, to a continuous adapted $X$, and the key estimate gives $X = \Phi(X)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: ex
[Example 4.6 — Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process and geometric Brownian motion]{.tag}

*Ornstein–Uhlenbeck.* Let $dX_t = -\theta X_t\, dt + \sigma\, dB_t$ with $\theta > 0$. Itô's formula gives $d(e^{\theta t} X_t) = \sigma e^{\theta t} dB_t$, hence
$$
X_t = e^{-\theta t} X_0 + \sigma \int_0^t e^{-\theta (t-s)}\, dB_s .
$$
Given $X_0 = x$, the Wiener integral is Gaussian (ch. 3.2), so
$$
X_t \sim \mathcal N\Big( e^{-\theta t} x,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta} \big(1 - e^{-2\theta t}\big) \Big) \ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal N\Big(0, \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\Big).
$$

*Geometric Brownian motion.* Let $dX_t = \mu X_t\, dt + \sigma X_t\, dB_t$ with $X_0 > 0$. Itô's formula for $\log X_t$ gives $d \log X_t = (\mu - \sigma^2/2)\, dt + \sigma\, dB_t$, hence
$$
X_t = X_0 \exp\big( (\mu - \tfrac12 \sigma^2)\, t + \sigma B_t \big).
$$
By Proposition 2.2, $\mathbb E X_t = X_0 e^{\mu t}$, yet $\frac1t \log X_t \to \mu - \sigma^2/2$ almost surely.

With $\mu = 0.05$ and $\sigma = 0.4$, the mean grows like $e^{0.05 t}$ while almost every path tends to $0$, since $\mu - \sigma^2/2 = -0.03$.
::::

### 4.4 The Euler–Maruyama scheme

Simulation replaces the SDE by the recursion, for a step $h$ and $k \ge 0$,
$$
X^h_{k+1} = X^h_k + h\, b(X^h_k) + \sigma(X^h_k) \big( B_{(k+1)h} - B_{kh} \big), \qquad X^h_0 = \xi .
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.7 — Strong order one half]{.tag} Under the assumptions of Theorem 4.5, there is a constant $C$, depending on $L$, $T$, $\mathbb E|\xi|^2$, $|b(0)|$ and $\|\sigma(0)\|_F$, such that
$$
\mathbb E \max_{k \le T/h} \big| X_{kh} - X^h_k \big|^2 \le C\, h .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* With $\eta(s) = h \lfloor s / h \rfloor$, the interpolation
$$
\bar X_t = \xi + \int_0^t b(\bar X_{\eta(s)})\, ds + \int_0^t \sigma(\bar X_{\eta(s)})\, dB_s
$$
equals $X^h_k$ at $t = kh$.

-   Over one step, drift and noise move $\bar X$ by $O(h)$ and $O(\sqrt h)$ in $L^2$: $\mathbb E|\bar X_s - \bar X_{\eta(s)}|^2 \le C_1 h$.
-   The key estimate of Theorem 4.5, with
    $$
    |b(X_s) - b(\bar X_{\eta(s)})| \le L(|X_s - \bar X_s| + |\bar X_s - \bar X_{\eta(s)}|)
    $$
    and the same for $\sigma$, gives $e(t) \le 2K \int_0^t e(s)\, ds + 2K C_1 T h$ for $e(t) = \mathbb E \sup_{s \le t} |X_s - \bar X_s|^2$.
-   Gronwall's lemma concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The *weak* error is of order $h$: $|\mathbb E f(X_T) - \mathbb E f(X^h_{T/h})| \le C h$ for smooth $f$ (Talay and Tubaro, 1990). Sampling cares about the weak error; ch. 7 measures it on the invariant law.

::: ex
[Example 4.8 — Measuring the strong order]{.tag} For geometric Brownian motion the exact solution is known (Example 4.6), so the error is computed path by path, with the same Brownian increments.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
mu, sigma, x0, T = 1.0, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0
n_paths, n_fine = 5_000, 2 ** 10
dW = rng.standard_normal((n_paths, n_fine)) * np.sqrt(T / n_fine)
exact = x0 * np.exp((mu - sigma**2 / 2) * T + sigma * dW.sum(axis=1))   # closed-form GBM at time T
hs, errs = [], []
for k in [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]:
    m = 2 ** k
    incr = dW.reshape(n_paths, m, -1).sum(axis=2)       # the same Brownian path on a coarser grid
    x = np.full(n_paths, x0)
    for j in range(m):                                  # Euler-Maruyama
        x = x + mu * x * (T / m) + sigma * x * incr[:, j]
    hs.append(T / m)
    errs.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((x - exact) ** 2)))
    print(f"h = 2^-{k:<2d}  strong L2 error at T = {errs[-1]:.4f}")
print(f"fitted order: {np.polyfit(np.log(hs), np.log(errs), 1)[0]:.2f}")
```

The errors are 1.197, 0.521, 0.234, 0.110 and 0.053 for $h = 2^{-2}, \dots, 2^{-10}$: dividing $h$ by 4 roughly halves the error. The fitted order is
$$
0.56 \approx \tfrac12 .
$$
:::

### 4.5 Generator, Kolmogorov and Fokker–Planck equations

Here $X$ solves $dX_t = b(X_t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t)\, dB_t$ with Lipschitz coefficients, $a = \sigma \sigma^\top$, and $X^x$ starts at $x$.

::: def
[Definition 4.9 — Generator]{.tag} The generator of the diffusion is the second-order operator
$$
\mathcal L f(x) = b(x) \cdot \nabla f(x) + \frac12 \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}(x)\, \partial_{ij} f(x), \qquad f \in C^2 .
$$
Its formal adjoint acts on densities:
$$
\mathcal L^* p = - \sum_i \partial_i (b_i\, p) + \frac12 \sum_{i,j} \partial_{ij} (a_{ij}\, p) .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.10 — Dynkin's formula]{.tag} For $f \in C^2_c(\mathbb R^d)$, the process
$$
M^f_t = f(X_t) - f(X_0) - \int_0^t \mathcal L f(X_s)\, ds
$$
is a martingale. In particular,
$$
\frac{d}{dt} \mathbb E f(X_t) = \mathbb E\, \mathcal L f(X_t).
$$

::: proof
By Itô's formula, $M^f_t = \int_0^t \nabla f(X_s)^\top \sigma(X_s)\, dB_s$, whose integrand is bounded ($\nabla f$ has compact support, $\sigma$ is continuous): a true martingale (Theorem 3.4). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.11 — Kolmogorov backward equation]{.tag} Let $g$ be bounded and continuous, and $u(t, x) = \mathbb E\, g(X^x_t)$. If $u \in C^{1,2}$ with bounded derivatives, then
$$
\partial_t u = \mathcal L u, \qquad u(0, \cdot) = g .
$$
This regularity holds when $b$, $\sigma$ and $g$ are smooth with bounded derivatives (Øksendal, Theorem 8.1.1; Pavliotis, ch. 2).

::: proof
Fix $t$. By the Markov property, $N_s = u(t - s, X^x_s) = \mathbb E[g(X^x_t) \mid \mathcal F_s]$ for $s \le t$ is a martingale. Itô's formula writes $N$ as a local martingale plus
$$
\int_0^s (-\partial_t u + \mathcal L u)(t - r, X^x_r)\, dr .
$$
This integral is a local martingale of finite variation, hence zero (Proposition 2.10); its continuous integrand vanishes at $r = 0$, where $X^x_0 = x$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With a killing rate $V \ge 0$, the same proof gives the **Feynman–Kac formula**:
$$
u(t,x) = \mathbb E\big[g(X^x_t)\, e^{-\int_0^t V(X^x_s)\, ds}\big]
$$
solves $\partial_t u = \mathcal L u - V u$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.12 — Fokker–Planck equation]{.tag} If $X_t$ has a density $p_t(x)$, smooth in $(t, x)$, then
$$
\partial_t p_t = \mathcal L^* p_t .
$$
A probability density $\pi$ is invariant (if $X_0 \sim \pi$ then $X_t \sim \pi$ for all $t$) when $\mathcal L^* \pi = 0$.

::: proof
For $f \in C^\infty_c$, Proposition 4.10 and two integrations by parts give
$$
\int f\, \partial_t p_t\, dx = \frac{d}{dt} \int f\, p_t\, dx = \int (\mathcal L f)\, p_t\, dx = \int f\, \mathcal L^* p_t\, dx .
$$
There are no boundary terms ($f$ has compact support), and $f$ is arbitrary. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Corollary 4.13 — The overdamped Langevin diffusion]{.tag} Let $U \in C^2(\mathbb R^d)$ with $Z = \int e^{-U} dx < \infty$, and $\pi = e^{-U} / Z$. The diffusion
$$
dX_t = -\nabla U(X_t)\, dt + \sqrt 2\, dB_t
$$
has generator $\mathcal L f = \Delta f - \nabla U \cdot \nabla f$ and leaves $\pi$ invariant. It is reversible: for $f, g \in C^2_c$,
$$
\int g\, \mathcal L f\, d\pi = - \int \nabla f \cdot \nabla g\, d\pi = \int f\, \mathcal L g\, d\pi .
$$

::: proof
Here
$$
\mathcal L^* p = \nabla \cdot (p \nabla U) + \Delta p = \nabla \cdot (p\, \nabla U + \nabla p).
$$
For $p = \pi$, $\nabla \pi = -\pi \nabla U$, so the flux $\pi \nabla U + \nabla \pi$ vanishes.

For reversibility,
$$
e^{-U}(\Delta f - \nabla U \cdot \nabla f) = \nabla \cdot (e^{-U} \nabla f);
$$
one integration by parts against $g$ gives the symmetric form. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Ch. 7 starts here: to sample from $\pi \propto e^{-U}$, simulate this diffusion.

### 4.6 Diffusions in physics and biology

The course description stresses models of physics and biology; two classical ones use exactly the tools above.

:::: ex
[Example 4.14 — Langevin's Brownian particle and the Einstein relation]{.tag} A particle of mass $m$ in a fluid at temperature $\Theta$ feels a friction $-\gamma V$ and molecular kicks (Langevin, 1908):
$$
m\, dV_t = -\gamma V_t\, dt + \sqrt{2 \gamma k_B \Theta}\, dB_t ,
$$
with $k_B$ Boltzmann's constant: an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with rate $\gamma/m$ and noise $\sqrt{2\gamma k_B \Theta}/m$.

-   Its stationary law is $\mathcal N(0, k_B \Theta / m)$ (Example 4.6), the Maxwell distribution: friction and temperature fix the noise (fluctuation–dissipation).
-   At stationarity,
    $$
    \mathrm{Cov}(V_0, V_s) = (k_B \Theta / m)\, e^{-\gamma s / m},
    $$
    so the position $X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t V_s\, ds$ satisfies
    $$
    \frac{\mathrm{Var}(X_t - X_0)}{t} = \frac2t \int_0^t (t - s)\, \mathrm{Cov}(V_0, V_s)\, ds \ \longrightarrow\ 2D, \qquad D = \frac{k_B \Theta}{\gamma} .
    $$

This is Einstein's relation (1905). With a force $-\nabla U$ and negligible inertia, the position solves
$$
\gamma\, dX = -\nabla U(X)\, dt + \sqrt{2\gamma k_B \Theta}\, dB,
$$
with invariant law proportional to $e^{-U/(k_B\Theta)}$: Corollary 4.13 up to units.
::::

:::: ex
[Example 4.15 — The Wright–Fisher diffusion of population genetics]{.tag} In a haploid population of $N$ individuals, the frequency of a neutral allele changes by random resampling at each generation. In units of $N$ generations and for large $N$, it follows
$$
dX_t = \sqrt{X_t (1 - X_t)}\, dB_t, \qquad X_0 = x \in (0,1).
$$
The coefficient is not Lipschitz at $0$ and $1$, but Hölder of order $1/2$ suffices for pathwise uniqueness (Theorem 6.6).

-   *Fixation probability.* $X$ is a bounded martingale, absorbed in $\{0, 1\}$ at the time $\tau$, which is finite because its mean (next item) is finite. Hence $\mathbb P(X_\tau = 1) = \mathbb E X_\tau = x$ (Theorem 2.7).
-   *Mean fixation time.* By Dynkin's formula up to $\tau$, $u(x) = \mathbb E_x \tau$ solves $\frac12 x(1-x)\, u'' = -1$ with $u(0) = u(1) = 0$:
    $$
    u(x) = -2\big( x \log x + (1 - x) \log(1 - x) \big).
    $$

For $x = 1/2$, $u = 2 \log 2 \approx 1.39$: the allele is lost or fixed after about $1.39\, N$ generations on average.
::::

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 4**

-   Itô's formula is Taylor's formula to second order with $(dB)^2 = dt$; it gives stochastic exponentials and Lévy's characterisation.
-   Lipschitz SDEs have unique strong solutions; Euler–Maruyama has strong order $1/2$ and weak order $1$.
-   The generator gives Kolmogorov's backward equation for expectations and the Fokker–Planck equation for densities.
-   The Langevin diffusion leaves $\pi \propto e^{-U}$ invariant and is reversible.
:::

## 5. Girsanov's theorem and changes of measure {#ch5}

Changing the drift of a diffusion amounts to reweighting its paths, and Girsanov's theorem gives the weight. It yields likelihoods for diffusions, importance samplers, and the Kullback–Leibler formula between two diffusions behind the guarantees of ch. 7 and ch. 8.

### 5.1 Warm-up: shifting a Gaussian

Let $Z \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$ under $\mathbb P$ and define $\mathbb Q$ by $d\mathbb Q / d\mathbb P = e^{\theta Z - \theta^2/2}$. For every $u$,
$$
\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\, e^{iuZ} = e^{-\theta^2/2}\, \mathbb E\, e^{(\theta + iu) Z} = e^{iu\theta - u^2/2},
$$
so $Z \sim \mathcal N(\theta, 1)$ under $\mathbb Q$. Girsanov's theorem does this for every increment of a Brownian path, with a shift that may depend on the past.

### 5.2 Girsanov's theorem

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.1 — Girsanov]{.tag} Let $\theta$ be a progressive process in $\mathbb R^d$ with $\int_0^T |\theta_s|^2 ds < \infty$ almost surely, and
$$
Z_t = \exp\Big( \int_0^t \theta_s \cdot dB_s - \frac12 \int_0^t |\theta_s|^2\, ds \Big), \qquad t \le T .
$$
If $\mathbb E Z_T = 1$, then $\mathbb Q = Z_T \cdot \mathbb P$ is a probability measure equivalent to $\mathbb P$ on $\mathcal F_T$, and
$$
W_t = B_t - \int_0^t \theta_s\, ds \quad \text{is a } \mathbb Q\text{-Brownian motion on } [0, T].
$$

::: proof
1.  $Z = \mathcal E(\int \theta \cdot dB)$ is a positive supermartingale (Proposition 4.2); with constant mean $\mathbb E Z_T = 1$, it is a martingale on $[0,T]$.
2.  *Bayes' rule.*
    $$
    \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[Y_t \mid \mathcal F_s] = \mathbb E[Z_t Y_t \mid \mathcal F_s] / Z_s,
    $$
    so $Y$ is a $\mathbb Q$-local martingale when $ZY$ is a $\mathbb P$-local martingale.
3.  Itô's product rule, with $dZ = Z\, \theta \cdot dB$ and $d\langle Z, B^i \rangle = Z \theta^i dt$, gives
    $$
    d(Z W^i) = Z\, dB^i - Z \theta^i dt + W^i dZ + Z \theta^i dt = Z\, dB^i + W^i dZ ,
    $$
    a $\mathbb P$-local martingale. So each $W^i$ is a continuous $\mathbb Q$-local martingale.
4.  Brackets are limits in probability of sums of products of increments, a notion preserved by $\mathbb Q \ll \mathbb P$. Hence
    $$
    \langle W^i, W^j \rangle_t = \langle B^i, B^j \rangle_t = \delta_{ij} t
    $$
    under $\mathbb Q$, and Lévy's theorem (Theorem 4.3) concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — Novikov's condition]{.tag} If
$$
\mathbb E \exp\Big( \frac12 \int_0^T |\theta_s|^2\, ds \Big) < \infty ,
$$
then $\mathbb E Z_T = 1$. In particular this holds when $\theta$ is bounded.

::: proof
*Bounded case,* $|\theta| \le K$. Write
$$
Z_t^2 = \mathcal E(2\theta \cdot B)_t \exp\big(\int_0^t |\theta_s|^2 ds\big) \le e^{K^2 T}\, \mathcal E(2\theta \cdot B)_t.
$$
The stochastic exponential is a positive supermartingale, so $\mathbb E Z_\tau^2 \le e^{K^2 T}$ for every stopping time $\tau \le T$.

Along a localising sequence $\tau_n$, the variables $Z_{\tau_n \wedge T}$ are bounded in $L^2$, hence uniformly integrable. Therefore $\mathbb E Z_T = \lim_n \mathbb E Z_{\tau_n \wedge T} = 1$. The general case is Revuz and Yor, Proposition VIII.1.15. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A condition is needed: with $\theta \equiv 1$ on $[0, \infty)$, $Z_t \to 0$ almost surely (Example 2.8), and $Z_\infty = 0$ is no density.

### 5.3 Radon–Nikodym derivatives between diffusion laws

Let $\mathcal C = C([0,T], \mathbb R^d)$ with its canonical process $\omega_t$. For $i = 1, 2$, let $\mathbb P^i$ be the law on $\mathcal C$ of the solution of
$$
dX_t = b_i(t, X)\, dt + dB_t, \qquad X_0 \sim \nu ,
$$
where the drift $b_i(t, \omega)$ may depend on the path up to time $t$ (it is progressive). Let $\mathbb W^\nu$ be the law of $\xi + B$ with $\xi \sim \nu$ independent of $B$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.3 — Likelihood of a diffusion path]{.tag} Assume that the SDEs are well posed in law and that the exponential below has mean 1 under $\mathbb W^\nu$ (for instance, $b_i$ bounded). Then $\mathbb P^i$ is equivalent to $\mathbb W^\nu$, with
$$
\frac{d\mathbb P^i}{d\mathbb W^\nu}(\omega) = \exp\Big( \int_0^T b_i(t, \omega) \cdot d\omega_t - \frac12 \int_0^T |b_i(t, \omega)|^2\, dt \Big).
$$
Consequently, $d\mathbb P^1 / d\mathbb P^2$ is the ratio of the two densities.

::: proof
Under $\mathbb W^\nu$, $\omega_t - \omega_0$ is a Brownian motion. Let $\mathbb Q$ have the stated density.

By Theorem 5.1 with $\theta_t = b_i(t, \omega)$, the process $\omega_t - \omega_0 - \int_0^t b_i(s, \omega)\, ds$ is a $\mathbb Q$-Brownian motion. So under $\mathbb Q$ the canonical process solves the SDE with initial law $\nu$. Uniqueness in law, assumed in the statement, gives $\mathbb Q = \mathbb P^i$; ch. 6 studies when it holds. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Path-dependent drifts matter: the interpolation of an Euler scheme has drift $b(\omega_{kh})$ on $[kh, (k+1)h)$, so Theorem 5.3 compares an algorithm with the diffusion it discretises (ch. 7 and ch. 8).

:::: prop
[Corollary 5.4 — Kullback–Leibler divergence between two diffusions]{.tag} Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.3, and if $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P^1} \int_0^T |b_1 - b_2|^2 dt < \infty$, then
$$
\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb P^1 \,\|\, \mathbb P^2) = \frac12\, \mathbb E_{\mathbb P^1} \int_0^T \big| b_1(t, X) - b_2(t, X) \big|^2\, dt .
$$
If the initial laws differ, $\mathrm{KL}(\nu_1 \| \nu_2)$ is added.

With noise $\sigma\, dB_t$ for a constant invertible $\sigma$, replace $b_1 - b_2$ by $\sigma^{-1}(b_1 - b_2)$.

In particular, with noise $\sqrt 2\, dB_t$, the factor $\frac12$ becomes $\frac14$.

::: proof
Under $\mathbb P^1$, $d\omega_t = b_1\, dt + dW^1_t$ with $W^1$ a $\mathbb P^1$-Brownian motion. Substituting into the ratio of the densities of Theorem 5.3,
$$
\log \frac{d\mathbb P^1}{d\mathbb P^2} = \int_0^T (b_1 - b_2) \cdot dW^1_t + \int_0^T \Big( (b_1 - b_2) \cdot b_1 - \tfrac12 |b_1|^2 + \tfrac12 |b_2|^2 \Big) dt .
$$
The second integrand equals $\frac12 |b_1 - b_2|^2$. The stochastic integral has mean $0$ under the integrability assumption (Theorem 3.4). With different initial laws, condition on $\omega_0$ and use the chain rule of the KL divergence. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — the KL divergence between two diffusions with the same noise]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathrm{Law}(X^1_T) \,\|\, \mathrm{Law}(X^2_T)\big) \le \mathrm{KL}(\mathbb P^1 \| \mathbb P^2) = \frac12\, \mathbb E \int_0^T |b_1 - b_2|^2(t, X^1)\, dt
$$
:::

The inequality on the left is data processing: mapping a path to its value at time $T$ cannot increase the divergence. A drift error along the path thus bounds the error of the final sample.

### 5.4 Likelihood ratios and importance sampling

:::: ex
[Example 5.5 — Estimating the drift of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process]{.tag} We observe a continuous path of $dX_t = -\theta X_t\, dt + dB_t$ on $[0, T]$ and want $\theta > 0$. By Theorem 5.3 with $b(x) = -\theta x$, the log-likelihood with respect to Wiener measure is
$$
\ell_T(\theta) = -\theta \int_0^T X_t\, dX_t - \frac{\theta^2}{2} \int_0^T X_t^2\, dt .
$$
It is maximised at
$$
\hat\theta_T = - \frac{\int_0^T X_t\, dX_t}{\int_0^T X_t^2\, dt}, \qquad \hat\theta_T - \theta = - \frac{\int_0^T X_t\, dB_t}{\int_0^T X_t^2\, dt} .
$$

The numerator is a martingale with bracket $\int_0^T X_t^2\, dt$, and the ergodic theorem gives $\frac1T \int_0^T X_t^2 dt \to 1/(2\theta)$. Hence $\hat\theta_T \to \theta$, and the martingale central limit theorem gives $\sqrt T(\hat\theta_T - \theta) \to \mathcal N(0, 2\theta)$ (Exercise 9).
::::

The diffusion coefficient is different. For $dX = \sigma\, dB$, one observed path on $[0,T]$ has quadratic variation exactly $\sigma^2 T$ (Theorem 1.8). The laws for two values of $\sigma$ are **mutually singular**: no likelihood ratio exists, and $\sigma$ is read off a single path without error.

:::: ex
[Example 5.6 — Importance sampling of a rare event]{.tag} We estimate, for $a = 4$,
$$
p = \mathbb P\Big(\max_{t \le 1} B_t \ge a\Big) = 2\, \mathbb P(B_1 \ge a) = 6.334 \times 10^{-5}
$$
(Proposition 1.7). Crude Monte Carlo with $2 \times 10^4$ paths sees the event about once.

Under $d\mathbb Q / d\mathbb P = e^{a B_1 - a^2/2}$, Theorem 5.1 with $\theta \equiv a$ gives $B_t = W_t + a t$ for a $\mathbb Q$-Brownian motion $W$; more than half of the paths now reach $a$, and
$$
p = \mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}\Big[ \mathbf 1_{\{\max_t B_t \ge a\}}\, e^{-a B_1 + a^2/2} \Big].
$$

Paths use a grid of 200 steps. Between two grid values $x, y < a$, a Brownian bridge reaches $a$ with probability $e^{-2(a-x)(a-y)/dt}$ (reflection principle); a constant drift does not change the bridge, so this removes the discretisation bias.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
a, n, n_paths = 4.0, 200, 20_000
dt = 1.0 / n
# Crude Monte Carlo of P(B_1 > a): about 0.6 successes expected
crude = np.mean(rng.standard_normal(n_paths) > a)
# Importance sampling: simulate under Q, where B_t = W_t + a t, and reweight by dP/dQ
dB = a * dt + np.sqrt(dt) * rng.standard_normal((n_paths, n))
B = np.hstack([np.zeros((n_paths, 1)), np.cumsum(dB, axis=1)])
w = np.exp(-a * B[:, -1] + a**2 / 2)                       # Girsanov weight on F_1
x0, x1 = B[:, :-1], B[:, 1:]
p_cross = np.where((x0 < a) & (x1 < a), np.exp(-2 * (a - x0) * (a - x1) / dt), 1.0)
hit = 1 - np.prod(1 - p_cross, axis=1)                      # P(the bridge reaches a | grid values)
for name, est, exact in [("P(B_1 > a)      ", w * (B[:, -1] > a), norm.sf(a)),
                         ("P(max B_t >= a) ", w * hit, 2 * norm.sf(a))]:
    m, se = est.mean(), est.std() / np.sqrt(n_paths)
    print(f"{name} IS = {m:.4e} +/- {1.96 * se:.1e}   exact = {exact:.4e}")
print(f"crude Monte Carlo of P(B_1 > a) with {n_paths} draws: {crude:.1e}")
```

The importance-sampling estimates, with 95 % half-widths, are $3.226 \times 10^{-5} \pm 0.093 \times 10^{-5}$ for $\mathbb P(B_1 > 4)$ (exact $3.167 \times 10^{-5}$) and $6.363 \times 10^{-5} \pm 0.27 \times 10^{-5}$ for the maximum (exact $6.334 \times 10^{-5}$).

Crude Monte Carlo returns $0$; it would need about $10^8$ draws for the same 3 % precision.
::::

The zero-variance change of measure is the conditional law given the event: a diffusion whose extra drift is the gradient of the log-probability of the event given the current state (a Doob h-transform). The reverse drift of diffusion models (ch. 8) has the same structure.

::: recap
**Key takeaways — chapter 5**

-   Reweighting by $\mathcal E(\int \theta \cdot dB)_T$ adds the drift $\int \theta\, ds$ to Brownian motion, if the exponential has mean 1 (Novikov).
-   Same noise, different drifts: equivalent laws with an explicit density; different noise levels: mutually singular laws.
-   The KL divergence between two such diffusions is half the integrated squared drift difference; it bounds the KL of the marginals.
-   Likelihood ratios give drift estimators; drift changes give importance samplers.
:::

## 6. Martingale problems, weak and strong solutions {#ch6}

Theorem 4.5 builds a solution from a given Brownian motion, but some equations have no such solution. This chapter separates what a solution is from how it is built: weak solutions, the martingale problem of Stroock and Varadhan, and the Yamada–Watanabe theorems.

### 6.1 Weak solutions and Tanaka's equation

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Weak solution, uniqueness in law]{.tag} A weak solution of $dX_t = b(X_t)\, dt + \sigma(X_t)\, dB_t$ with initial law $\mu$ is a filtered probability space carrying a Brownian motion $B$ and a continuous adapted $X$ with $X_0 \sim \mu$ that satisfy the integral equation. The space and the Brownian motion are part of the solution.

-   **Uniqueness in law** holds if all weak solutions with initial law $\mu$ have the same law on $C([0, \infty), \mathbb R^d)$.
-   **Pathwise uniqueness** (Definition 4.4) compares two solutions on the same space with the same $B$ and the same $X_0$.
:::

:::: ex
[Example 6.2 — Tanaka's equation]{.tag} Let $\mathrm{sgn}(x) = 1$ for $x > 0$ and $-1$ for $x \le 0$, and consider
$$
dX_t = \mathrm{sgn}(X_t)\, dB_t, \qquad X_0 = 0 .
$$

-   *Weak existence.* For a Brownian motion $X$, $B_t = \int_0^t \mathrm{sgn}(X_s)\, dX_s$ has bracket $t$, so it is a Brownian motion (Lévy), and $dX = \mathrm{sgn}(X)\, dB$ since $\mathrm{sgn}^2 = 1$.
-   *Uniqueness in law.* Every solution is a continuous local martingale with bracket $t$: a Brownian motion.
-   *No pathwise uniqueness.* $-X$ solves the equation with the same $B$: the signs differ only on the Lebesgue-null set of times where $X_t = 0$.
-   *No strong solution.* Tanaka's formula extends Itô's formula to the function $|x|$, by smoothing it:
    $$
    |X_t| = \int_0^t \mathrm{sgn}(X_s)\, dX_s + L_t, \qquad L_t = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{2\varepsilon} \int_0^t \mathbf 1_{\{|X_s| < \varepsilon\}}\, ds .
    $$
    The local time $L$ measures the time that $X$ spends near $0$ (Revuz and Yor, ch. VI.1). The integral is $B_t$, so $B_t = |X_t| - L_t$ is a functional of $|X|$.

    The sign of $X$, independent of $|X|$, is therefore not a function of $B$: it is extra randomness (Revuz and Yor, ch. IX.1).
::::

Weak existence and uniqueness in law can thus hold without strong existence; for sampling, only the *law* matters.

### 6.2 The martingale problem

By Dynkin's formula (Proposition 4.10), $f(X_t) - \int_0^t \mathcal L f(X_s)\, ds$ is a martingale. Stroock and Varadhan made this the *definition* of a diffusion with generator $\mathcal L$.

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Martingale problem]{.tag} Let $b$ and $a$ be measurable and locally bounded, with $a(x)$ symmetric non-negative, and let $\mathcal L$ be as in Definition 4.9.

A probability $\mathbb P$ on $C([0,\infty), \mathbb R^d)$ with canonical process $X$ **solves the martingale problem** $\mathrm{MP}(b, a, \mu)$ if $X_0 \sim \mu$ and, for every $f \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R^d)$,
$$
M^f_t = f(X_t) - f(X_0) - \int_0^t \mathcal L f(X_s)\, ds
$$
is a $\mathbb P$-martingale for the canonical filtration. The problem is **well posed** if it has exactly one solution for every initial law.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.4 — Martingale problems and weak solutions]{.tag} Let $\sigma$ satisfy $\sigma \sigma^\top = a$. A probability $\mathbb P$ solves $\mathrm{MP}(b, a, \mu)$ if and only if it is the law of a weak solution of $dX = b(X)\, dt + \sigma(X)\, dB$ with $X_0 \sim \mu$. In particular, uniqueness in law for the SDE is the same as uniqueness for the martingale problem.

::: proof
*Weak solution ⇒ martingale problem.* This is Dynkin's formula, whose proof only used Itô's formula.

*Martingale problem ⇒ weak solution, for $\sigma$ invertible.* Localise with the exit times $\tau_R$ of balls, so that $f(x) = x_i$ and $f(x) = x_i x_j$ may be used.

-   With $f = x_i$: the process $M = X - X_0 - \int_0^\cdot b(X_s)\, ds$ is a continuous local martingale, so $X$ is a semimartingale.
-   With $f = x_i x_j$: the process $X^i X^j - \int_0^\cdot (X^i b_j + X^j b_i + a_{ij})(X_s)\, ds$ is a local martingale. Itô's product rule writes $X^i X^j$ as a local martingale plus $\int (X^i b_j + X^j b_i)\, ds + \langle M^i, M^j \rangle$.
-   Subtracting, $\langle M^i, M^j \rangle - \int a_{ij}(X_s)\, ds$ is a local martingale of finite variation, hence zero (Proposition 2.10).
-   Let $B = \int \sigma(X_s)^{-1} dM_s$. Its brackets are $\int \sigma^{-1} a\, \sigma^{-\top} ds = t\, I$, so $B$ is a Brownian motion (Theorem 4.3). Finally $dX = b(X)\, dt + dM = b(X)\, dt + \sigma(X)\, dB$.

If $\sigma$ is degenerate, the same proof works on an enlarged space carrying an independent Brownian motion (Karatzas and Shreve, Proposition 5.4.6). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The formulation pays off in three ways.

-   **Existence by compactness.** Laws of approximations (Euler schemes) are tight on path space, and limit points solve the martingale problem.
-   **Uniqueness gives the Markov property.** $\mathrm{MP}(b, a)$ is well posed when $a$ is bounded, continuous and uniformly elliptic and $b$ is bounded measurable (Stroock and Varadhan, 1979); its solutions form a strong Markov family.
-   **Diffusion limits of algorithms.** If the generators of rescaled Markov chains converge to $\mathcal L$, their laws converge to the solution of $\mathrm{MP}(b,a)$; random-walk Metropolis in high dimension thus behaves like a Langevin diffusion (Roberts, Gelman and Gilks, 1997).

### 6.3 From weak to strong: the Yamada–Watanabe theorems

::: thm
